   - Model Output: TP = 24, TN = 60, FP = 10, FN = 6
   - Total Classification Errors: FP + FN = 10 + 6 = 16 errors
   - Aggregate Accuracy: (24 + 60) / 100 = 84% (0.84)

2. Impact on Precision (Penalizing False Positives):
   - Total Meters Flagged for Theft = TP + FP = 24 + 10 = 34
   - Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 24 / (24 + 10) = 24 / 34 ≈ 70.59%
   - Consequence: Out of 34 field audits dispatched, 10 (29.4%) were wasteful false alarms.

3. Impact on Recall (Penalizing False Negatives):
   - Total Actual Theft Meters = TP + FN = 24 + 6 = 30
   - Recall (Sensitivity) = TP / (TP + FN) = 24 / (24 + 6) = 24 / 30 = 80.00%
   - Consequence: The model successfully caught 80% of theft, but 6 theft cases (20%) leaked unbilled power.

4. Adjusting the Decision Threshold (tau):
   - Case A (Conservative tau = 0.70):
     * Flags only obvious theft cases: TP drops to 18, FP drops to 2.
     * Precision jumps to 18 / 20 = 90.0%, but Recall plunges to 18 / 30 = 60.0% (12 missed thefts).
   - Case B (Aggressive tau = 0.30):
     * Flags any suspicious fluctuation: TP rises to 28, FN drops to 2.
     * Recall surges to 28 / 30 = 93.3%, but FP rises to 22, dropping Precision to 28 / 50 = 56.0%.

quick_types.name: False Positive (Type I Error)
quick_types.description: The model predicts positive on an actual negative instance, triggering a false alarm.

quick_types.name: False Negative (Type II Error)
quick_types.description: The model predicts negative on an actual positive instance, missing the target event.

quick_types.name: Precision-Optimized Regime
quick_types.description: A high-threshold setting prioritizing alert reliability and minimizing false alarms.

quick_types.name: Recall-Optimized Regime
quick_types.description: A low-threshold setting prioritizing maximum coverage and minimizing missed detections.

connected_logic.title: Asymmetric Error Cost Economics
points: In healthcare, a False Negative (missed cancer) is far deadlier than a False Positive biopsy.
In spam filtering, a False Positive (lost job offer) is worse than a missed spam email.
Optimizing machine learning requires calibrating models against real-world business losses.

connected_logic.title: Threshold Tuning Mechanics
points: Lowering threshold tau shifts predictions from negative to positive across ambiguous scores.
Reduces False Negatives and boosts Recall at the cost of generating more False Positives.
Raising threshold tau cleans up false alarms but increases the risk of missed detections.

connected_logic.title: Precision-Recall Seesaw Effect
points: Precision and Recall share an inverse relationship governed by classification thresholds.
Fixing True Positives while adding False Positives directly depresses Precision score.
Fixing True Positives while adding False Negatives directly depresses Recall score.

connected_logic.title: Scikit-Learn Evaluation Protocol
points: Always specify explicit label ordering: confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred, labels=[0, 1]).
Unpacking with .ravel() strictly follows the order: tn, fp, fn, tp.
Failing to pass labels can invert the matrix if only positive predictions are present.

pitfalls: Assuming error costs are symmetrical: Treating a false alarm as equal to a missed threat distorts decisions.
Sticking to the default 0.5 threshold: Default cutoffs ignore class imbalance and operational constraints.
Relying on accuracy on skewed data: 84% accuracy masks 16 critical mistakes in fraud and theft pipelines.
Confusing Type I and Type II terms: Type I is false alarm (alpha), while Type II is missed event (beta).
Ignoring alert fatigue: Flooding operations teams with excessive False Positives causes real alerts to be ignored.
key_takeaways: False Positives (Type I) are false alarms that degrade model Precision and waste investigative resources.
False Negatives (Type II) are missed events that degrade model Recall and leave hazards undetected.
Adjusting decision thresholds allows teams to trade off between False Positives and False Negatives.
Model performance must be judged by business cost rather than aggregate classification accuracy.

title: Precision (Positive Predictive Value)
def: A classification evaluation metric, also called Positive Predictive Value (PPV), that calculates the proportion of positive model predictions that are genuinely correct in ground truth.
definition: A classification evaluation metric, also called Positive Predictive Value (PPV), that calculates the proportion of positive model predictions that are genuinely correct in ground truth.
simple_summary: Precision measures the quality and trustworthiness of your model's alerts. If an electricity fraud model rings an alarm 100 times, precision tells you how many of those 100 alarms were real thieves rather than innocent people. High precision means when the model speaks, you can trust it.
definition_bullets: Calculates the ratio of True Positives to all model-predicted positive cases.
Also known across statistics and medicine as Positive Predictive Value (PPV).
Heavily penalizes False Positives (Type I errors or false alarms).
Does not measure how many positive cases were missed by the model.

core_terms.what_is_it: The percentage of positive claims made by the model that were actually correct.
core_terms.definition: Precision is the classification metric defined as the ratio of True Positives to the sum of True Positives and False Positives (TP / (TP + FP)).
core_terms.analogy: The percentage of suspect arrests made by police that turn out to be actual criminals.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Critical when every positive prediction triggers an expensive action, audit, or irreversible consequence.

core_terms.what_is_it: Target cases that the model correctly identified as positive.
core_terms.definition: Instances belonging to the positive class that the model accurately labeled as positive.
core_terms.analogy: Correctly identifying an actual theft meter during an inspection.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Forms the numerator of precision, measuring successful positive identifications.

core_terms.what_is_it: Innocent cases that the model mistakenly flagged as positive.
core_terms.definition: Negative instances mistakenly assigned a positive prediction by the classifier.
core_terms.analogy: Dispatching an audit crew to an honest customer who did nothing wrong.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Forms the error penalty in the precision denominator, degrading alert reliability.

core_terms.what_is_it: The exact complement of precision, measuring the proportion of alerts that are false alarms.
core_terms.definition: False Discovery Rate (FDR) equals 1 - Precision, or FP / (TP + FP).
core_terms.analogy: The percentage of false fire alarms received by a municipal fire station.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Directly quantifies operational waste from chasing bad model leads.

core_terms.what_is_it: The probability level a sample must cross to be labeled as positive.
core_terms.definition: The boundary value (e.g., 0.50 or 0.80) that transforms continuous predicted probabilities into positive classifications.
core_terms.analogy: Setting the minimum score required to pass a strict security clearance.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Raising the threshold filters out uncertain predictions, typically boosting precision.

symbol_guide.description: Fraction of positive predictions that are genuine: TP / (TP + FP).
Statistical and medical terminology synonymous with Precision.
Count of positive instances correctly classified as positive.
Count of negative instances mistakenly classified as positive.
Total volume of positive alarms generated by the classifier.
Complement of precision: FP / (TP + FP) = 1 - Precision.
Probability threshold applied to convert scores into binary predictions.

logic: Precision evaluates the purity of a model's positive predictions without considering unflagged cases. It ignores True Negatives and False Negatives entirely. Therefore, a model that makes only two positive predictions and gets both right achieves 100% precision, even if it ignored 1,000 other positive cases. Precision is essential whenever positive predictions trigger costly downstream operations, such as dispatching field engineers, blocking credit cards, or initiating medical biopsies.
example: A utility company deploys Model A (90% precision) and Model B (60% precision) to detect electricity theft. Each field inspection costs $150 in truck rolls and technician labor. Dispatching 100 audits under Model A yields 90 confirmed thefts and 10 wasted trips ($1,500 wasted). Dispatching 100 audits under Model B yields only 60 thefts and 40 wasted trips ($6,000 wasted). Higher precision directly protects operational budgets.
numerical_example:
Step-by-Step Worked Example (Electricity Theft Audit Pipeline):

1. Dataset Evaluation (N = 1,000 Meters):
   - True Positives (TP): 80 (confirmed thefts detected)
   - False Positives (FP): 20 (honest meters wrongly flagged)
   - True Negatives (TN): 850 (normal meters left alone)
   - False Negatives (FN): 50 (thefts that went undetected)
   - Total Predictions Flagged as Positive: TP + FP = 80 + 20 = 100

2. Precision (PPV) Calculation:
   - Precision = TP / (TP + FP)
   - Precision = 80 / (80 + 20) = 80 / 100 = 0.80 (80.0%)
   - Interpretation: 80% of flagged meters are genuine theft; 20% are false alarms.

3. Comparative Model Audit (100 Flagged Alerts Each):
   - Model A: TP = 90, FP = 10 -> Precision = 90 / 100 = 90.0%
   - Model B: TP = 60, FP = 40 -> Precision = 60 / 100 = 60.0%
   - Operational Impact: Model A wastes only 10 inspection visits vs 40 for Model B.

4. Decision Threshold Tuning on 5 Sample Meters:
   - Meter A: 92% prob -> Flagged at tau = 0.50
   - Meter B: 81% prob -> Flagged at tau = 0.50
   - Meter C: 67% prob -> Flagged at tau = 0.50
   - Meter D: 48% prob -> Not flagged at tau = 0.50
   - Meter E: 32% prob -> Not flagged at tau = 0.50
   - At tau = 0.50: 3 meters flagged. Raising tau to 0.75 drops Meter C, keeping only high-confidence alerts (A & B) to maximize precision.

quick_types.name: High Precision Regime (>90%)
quick_types.description: Alerts are highly trusted; used when false alarms incur heavy financial or legal penalties.

quick_types.name: Balanced Regime (70% - 85%)
quick_types.description: Standard operating point balancing alert reliability with reasonable target coverage.

quick_types.name: Low Precision Regime (<60%)
quick_types.description: Accepts many false alarms to ensure rare, catastrophic events are rarely missed.

quick_types.name: Micro vs Macro Precision
quick_types.description: Multi-class aggregation either pooling global TP/FP or averaging class-wise precision equally.

connected_logic.title: Precision vs Recall Divergence
points: Precision measures prediction purity: TP / (TP + FP).
Recall measures ground truth coverage: TP / (TP + FN).
A model flagging 1 item correctly has 100% precision but near 0% recall.

connected_logic.title: Threshold Sensitivity Behavior
points: Raising threshold tau demands higher probability before positive classification.
Eliminates low-confidence false positives, generally increasing precision.
May drop borderline true positives, sacrificing overall recall.

connected_logic.title: Downstream Cost Justification
points: Prioritize precision when taking action on a positive alert costs money.
Used in spam folders, automated account bans, and court evidence pipelines.
Prevents alert fatigue among human investigation and audit teams.

connected_logic.title: Scikit-Learn Implementation Standard
points: Calculated via precision_score(y_true, y_pred, zero_division=0).
Passing zero_division=0 prevents crashes when zero positive predictions occur.
For multi-class, specify average='macro', 'micro', or 'weighted'.

pitfalls: Assuming 100% precision implies a good model: A model flagging only 1 obvious case misses everything else.
Ignoring zero-division errors: If a model predicts zero positives, precision has a zero denominator.
Optimizing precision in safety-critical tasks: Maximizing precision in cancer screening causes lethal missed tumors.
Confusing precision with accuracy: Accuracy evaluates all predictions; precision only evaluates positive claims.
Believing threshold increases always raise precision: On irregular probability distributions, precision can fluctuate non-monotonically.
key_takeaways: Precision measures the fraction of positive predictions that are genuinely correct.
Focus on precision when the cost of a false alarm is significantly higher than a missed case.
Precision depends solely on True Positives and False Positives, ignoring True Negatives completely.
Always evaluate precision alongside recall to ensure adequate coverage of real-world events.

title: Recall / Sensitivity (True Positive Rate)
def: A classification evaluation metric, also known as Sensitivity or True Positive Rate (TPR), that measures the proportion of genuine positive cases that a model successfully identifies.
definition: A classification evaluation metric, also known as Sensitivity or True Positive Rate (TPR), that measures the proportion of genuine positive cases that a model successfully identifies.
simple_summary: Recall answers: 'Did we catch them all?' In electricity theft detection, if 100 people are secretly stealing power, recall tells you how many of those 100 thieves were caught. High recall means very few offenders slipped past your system unnoticed, even if you accidentally inspected a few innocent meters along the way.
definition_bullets: Calculates the proportion of actual ground-truth positive cases correctly detected.
Commonly referred to as Sensitivity in medicine and True Positive Rate (TPR) in statistics.
Directly penalizes False Negatives (Type II errors or missed detections).
Complementary to False Negative Rate (FNR), satisfying the relationship Recall + FNR = 1.

core_terms.what_is_it: The percentage of real positive instances that the model successfully caught.
core_terms.definition: Recall is the classification metric defined as the ratio of True Positives to the sum of True Positives and False Negatives (TP / (TP + FN)).
core_terms.analogy: A fishing net catching 80 out of 100 fish swimming in a pond.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Essential when missing an occurrence carries severe financial, legal, or health risks.

core_terms.what_is_it: The percentage of real positive cases that slipped past the model undetected.
core_terms.definition: False Negative Rate is the ratio of False Negatives to all actual positives (FN / (TP + FN)), exactly equaling 1 - Recall.
core_terms.analogy: The percentage of fish that escaped through holes in the fishing net.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Directly quantifies leakage and security vulnerabilities in detection systems.

core_terms.what_is_it: Actual positive cases that were correctly caught and flagged by the model.
core_terms.definition: Ground truth positive instances accurately assigned a positive class prediction.
core_terms.analogy: The 80 meters with illegal bypasses that the inspection model caught.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Forms the numerator of recall, representing successful case recoveries.

core_terms.what_is_it: Real positive cases that were mistakenly labeled as normal or negative.
core_terms.definition: Ground truth positive instances that the model erroneously classified as negative.
core_terms.analogy: The 20 power thieves who continued stealing electricity without being detected.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Drives the penalty in the recall denominator, directly eroding detection coverage.

core_terms.what_is_it: An architecture using a high-recall filter first, followed by a high-precision verifier.
core_terms.definition: A production design where an initial model maximizes recall to catch all suspects, followed by a precise secondary test that eliminates false alarms.
core_terms.analogy: An airport metal detector screening everyone, followed by a physical wand check for those who beep.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Enables systems to achieve near 100% recall without overwhelming operations with permanent false alarms.

symbol_guide.description: Proportion of all real positive instances identified: TP / (TP + FN).
Clinical and biomedical term identical to Recall.
Statistical terminology denoting Recall.
Proportion of positive instances missed: FN / (TP + FN) = 1 - Recall.
Count of positive cases correctly classified by the model.
Count of positive cases mistakenly classified as negative.
The true ground-truth volume of all positive instances in existence.
Probability threshold applied to convert scores into binary predictions.

logic: Recall measures coverage rather than prediction purity. It evaluates what fraction of real-world positive events were discovered. It completely ignores False Positives and True Negatives. A trivial model that predicts positive for every single sample in the universe achieves 100% recall because it misses zero positive cases (FN = 0), even though its precision is abysmal. Recall is prioritized whenever the penalty for a missed detection (such as an undetected cancer tumor or unbilled electricity theft) far exceeds the cost of investigating a false alarm.
example: A power utility company monitors 10,000 smart meters. Undetected electricity bypasses leak $2,000 per meter annually, whereas sending a technician to investigate an innocent meter costs only $50. If Model A achieves 95% recall with 70% precision, while Model B achieves 60% recall with 95% precision, Model A is dramatically superior: it prevents $70,000 in unbilled power theft while incurring only minor inspection overhead.
numerical_example:
Step-by-Step Worked Example (Electricity Theft Audit Pipeline):

1. Dataset Ground Truth & Outcomes (N = 1,000 Meters):
   - True Positives (TP): 80 (confirmed theft detected)
   - False Negatives (FN): 20 (actual theft missed by model)
   - False Positives (FP): 40 (normal meters wrongly flagged)
   - True Negatives (TN): 860 (normal meters correctly cleared)
   - Total Actual Ground-Truth Theft Cases: TP + FN = 80 + 20 = 100

2. Recall (Sensitivity / TPR) Calculation:
   - Recall = TP / (TP + FN)
   - Recall = 80 / (80 + 20) = 80 / 100 = 0.80 (80.0%)
   - Interpretation: The system caught 80 out of 100 thieves (80% coverage).

3. False Negative Rate (FNR) Calculation:
   - FNR = FN / (TP + FN) = 20 / 100 = 0.20 (20.0%)
   - Verifying Complementarity: Recall + FNR = 80% + 20% = 100% (1.0).

4. Decision Threshold Simulation Across 6 Illustrative Meters:
   - Actual Theft: Meter A (92%), Meter B (81%), Meter D (48%), Meter F (18%) -> 4 Total Thefts
   - Actual Normal: Meter C (67%), Meter E (32%) -> 2 Normal
   - Case 1 (Standard Cutoff tau = 0.50):
     * Flagged (prob >= 0.50): Meters A (TP), B (TP), C (FP).
     * Missed (prob < 0.50): Meters D (FN), F (FN).
     * TP = 2, FN = 2 -> Recall = 2 / (2 + 2) = 50.0% (2 thefts missed).
   - Case 2 (Aggressive Cutoff tau = 0.40):
     * Meter D (48%) is now flagged (converted from FN to TP).
     * TP = 3, FN = 1 -> Recall = 3 / 4 = 75.0% (Only 1 theft missed).

connected_logic.title: Recall vs Precision Penalty Dynamics
points: Recall penalizes False Negatives: misses destroy coverage.
Precision penalizes False Positives: false alarms destroy trust.
Predicting positive for every sample yields 100% recall but useless precision.

connected_logic.title: Threshold Tuning for Sensitivity
points: Lowering classification threshold tau captures ambiguous positive instances.
Converts borderline False Negatives into True Positives, boosting recall.
Concurrently increases False Positives, depressing precision.

connected_logic.title: Cascade Architecture Utility
points: Stage 1 uses a lightweight high-recall model to filter out obvious negatives.
Stage 2 deploys a heavy high-precision model to eliminate false positives.
Guarantees high overall recall without overwhelming downstream teams.

connected_logic.title: Scikit-Learn Implementation Standard
points: Calculated via recall_score(y_true, y_pred, zero_division=0).
For imbalanced data, evaluate recall alongside precision and PR-AUC.
Use average='macro' in multi-class problems to protect rare classes.

pitfalls: The all-positive prediction trap: Predicting positive on all cases achieves 100% recall with zero practical utility.
Blindness to False Positives: Recall does not care how many innocent users were harassed with false alarms.
Relying on accuracy on rare classes: 99% accuracy can easily hide 0% recall on 1% fraudulent transactions.
Confusing the denominator: Precision divides by predicted positives (TP+FP); Recall divides by actual positives (TP+FN).
Ignoring operational capacity: Maxing out recall without a triage mechanism overwhelms investigators with alerts.
key_takeaways: Recall measures the percentage of actual positive events the model successfully captured.
Prioritize recall when the cost of a missed detection is far greater than investigating a false alarm.
Recall and False Negative Rate always sum to 1.0 (Recall + FNR = 1).
Always evaluate recall in combination with precision or F1-score to assess true model effectiveness.

title: F1-Score (Harmonic Mean)
def: A classification evaluation metric that computes the harmonic mean of Precision and Recall, providing a single balanced performance score that heavily penalizes extreme trade-off disparities.
definition: A classification evaluation metric that computes the harmonic mean of Precision and Recall, providing a single balanced performance score that heavily penalizes extreme trade-off disparities.
simple_summary: Imagine a model that catches every thief but accuses half the city, or one that never makes a false accusation but lets most thieves escape. Neither is good. The F1-score combines precision and recall into a single grade. It can only be high if both precision and recall are strong at the same time.
definition_bullets: Combines Precision and Recall into a unified scalar performance index.
Calculated as the harmonic mean rather than the simple arithmetic average.
Heavily penalizes extreme imbalances between false alarms and missed detections.
Ideal for evaluating classifiers on imbalanced datasets where accuracy fails.

core_terms.what_is_it: A single score combining Precision and Recall using their harmonic mean.
core_terms.definition: The F1-score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, balancing positive predictive value and sensitivity into a unified metric bounded between 0.0 and 1.0.
core_terms.analogy: A student's composite grade that fails them if they completely flunk either math or science.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Provides a reliable single metric to rank and compare competing models on imbalanced data.

core_terms.what_is_it: A reciprocal-based mathematical average that pulls the result toward the lower of two values.
core_terms.definition: The reciprocal of the arithmetic mean of reciprocals, formulated for two numbers as 2xy / (x + y).
core_terms.analogy: A relay race team's speed being limited by the slowest runner rather than the fastest.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Prevents a model with 99% precision but 1% recall from claiming a misleading 50% average score.

core_terms.what_is_it: The proportion of positive model alerts that were actually genuine.
core_terms.definition: The ratio of True Positives to all model-predicted positive cases (TP / (TP + FP)).
core_terms.analogy: The percentage of fire alarms called that were real fires.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Ensures the model does not trigger excessive false alarms.

core_terms.what_is_it: The proportion of all real positive instances that the model successfully caught.
core_terms.definition: The ratio of True Positives to all actual ground-truth positive cases (TP / (TP + FN)).
core_terms.analogy: The percentage of all real fires in the city that were detected.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Ensures the model does not leave positive events undetected.

core_terms.what_is_it: A generalized F-score that weights precision or recall more heavily using a factor beta.
core_terms.definition: A weighted harmonic mean where beta controls emphasis: beta=2 favors recall twice as much as precision, while beta=0.5 favors precision.
core_terms.analogy: A grading scale where the final exam counts double compared to weekly homework.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Allows business stakeholders to align metric evaluation with asymmetric error costs.

symbol_guide.description: Harmonic mean balancing Precision and Recall equally: 2PR / (P + R).
Positive Predictive Value: TP / (TP + FP).
True Positive Rate / Sensitivity: TP / (TP + FN).
Correctly detected positive cases.
Negative cases incorrectly flagged as positive.
Positive cases incorrectly classified as negative.
Weighted harmonic mean adjusting relative importance between precision and recall.
Multiplier determining recall emphasis (beta=1 yields F1, beta=2 yields F2).

logic: Why harmonic mean instead of arithmetic average? If a model achieves 100% precision by predicting positive for only 1 sample, but achieves 0% recall by missing 10,000 cases, its arithmetic mean is (100% + 0%) / 2 = 50%. A 50% score suggests mediocre utility, yet the model is completely useless in production. The harmonic mean computes 2 * (1.0 * 0.0) / (1.0 + 0.0) = 0.0, accurately penalizing the failure. The harmonic mean forces both precision and recall to remain high simultaneously.
example: A power utility evaluates three models on 1,000 meters. Model A achieves 95% Precision and 40% Recall (F1 = 56.3%), rarely crying wolf but missing most theft. Model C achieves 40% Precision and 95% Recall (F1 = 56.3%), catching theft but overwhelming field staff with false alarms. Model B achieves 75% Precision and 75% Recall (F1 = 75.0%). Model B wins the deployment because its balanced performance yields high operational utility.
numerical_example:
Step-by-Step Worked Example (Electricity Theft Model Evaluation):

1. Dataset Evaluation (N = 1,000 Meters):
   - True Positives (TP): 80
   - False Positives (FP): 20
   - False Negatives (FN): 40
   - True Negatives (TN): 860
   - Total Predicted Positives: TP + FP = 80 + 20 = 100
   - Total Actual Positives: TP + FN = 80 + 40 = 120

2. Step 1: Precision Calculation:
   - Precision (P) = TP / (TP + FP) = 80 / (80 + 20) = 80 / 100 = 0.800 (80.0%)

3. Step 2: Recall Calculation:
   - Recall (R) = TP / (TP + FN) = 80 / (80 + 40) = 80 / 120 ≈ 0.667 (66.7%)

4. Step 3: F1-Score Calculation via Harmonic Mean:
   - F1 = 2 * (P * R) / (P + R)
   - F1 = 2 * (0.800 * 0.6667) / (0.800 + 0.6667)
   - F1 = 2 * (0.5333) / 1.4667 = 1.0667 / 1.4667 ≈ 0.727 (72.7%)

5. Step 4: Verification via Direct Confusion Matrix Formulation:
   - F1 = 2*TP / (2*TP + FP + FN)
   - F1 = 2*(80) / (2*80 + 20 + 40) = 160 / (160 + 60) = 160 / 220 ≈ 0.7273 (72.7%)

6. Harmonic vs Arithmetic Mean Comparison (P = 90%, R = 30%):
   - Arithmetic Mean = (90% + 30%) / 2 = 60.0% (misleadingly optimistic)
   - Harmonic Mean (F1) = 2 * (0.90 * 0.30) / (0.90 + 0.30) = 0.54 / 1.20 = 45.0%
   - Consequence: The severe deficiency in recall drags F1 down to 45.0%.

quick_types.description: Equally balances precision and recall using an unweighted harmonic mean.

quick_types.name: F2-Score (beta = 2.0)
quick_types.description: Weights recall twice as heavily as precision for safety and fraud detection.

quick_types.name: F0.5-Score (beta = 0.5)
quick_types.description: Weights precision twice as heavily as recall for search and spam filters.

connected_logic.title: Harmonic Mean Penalty Logic
points: Harmonic mean is always less than or equal to the geometric and arithmetic means.
If either precision or recall drops to 0, F1 crashes to 0.
Incentivizes machine learning optimizers to find a balanced operational sweet spot.

connected_logic.title: Class Imbalance Superiority
points: Accuracy is distorted by massive True Negative majorities.
F1 focuses exclusively on TP, FP, and FN, ignoring TN entirely.
Reflects true minority-class predictive capability in fraud and disease detection.

connected_logic.title: Cost Asymmetry Limitations
points: Standard F1 implicitly assumes false alarms and missed events cost the same.
When a missed cancer case costs 100x a false alarm, F1 is misleading.
Engineers switch to F2-Score or cost-matrix expected value optimization.

connected_logic.title: Scikit-Learn Implementation Standard
points: Computed via f1_score(y_true, y_pred, average='binary').
Multi-class classification supports average='macro', 'micro', or 'weighted'.
Pair with classification_report for a comprehensive precision-recall-f1 table.

pitfalls: Blindness to error direction: An F1 of 70% does not reveal whether precision or recall is the bottleneck.
Ignoring True Negatives: F1 does not reward models that successfully clear massive negative populations.
Equal cost assumption: Relying on F1 when missed cases cost far more than false alarms leads to suboptimal models.
Zero division in edge cases: If TP, FP, and FN are all zero, F1 is undefined without zero_division configuration.
Using macro F1 on extreme imbalance: Macro F1 weights a class with 3 samples identically to one with 100,000.
key_takeaways: The F1-score is the harmonic mean of Precision and Recall, balancing false alarms with missed detections.
Harmonic averaging ensures F1 is high only when both precision and recall are strong simultaneously.
F1 is far superior to Accuracy for evaluating models trained on imbalanced datasets.
Always inspect individual precision and recall values alongside F1 to diagnose model weaknesses.

title: Prediction Bias & Calibration
def: Diagnostic evaluation concepts in machine learning that verify whether a model's predicted outputs and probabilities faithfully reflect real-world frequencies, ensuring predictions are neither systematically skewed nor falsely overconfident.
definition: Diagnostic evaluation concepts in machine learning that verify whether a model's predicted outputs and probabilities faithfully reflect real-world frequencies, ensuring predictions are neither systematically skewed nor falsely overconfident.
simple_summary: If a weather forecast says there is a 70% chance of rain, it should actually rain on 70 out of 100 such days. If it only rains on 20 days, the forecast is overconfident and biased. Prediction bias checks if a model systematically over- or under-predicts on average, while calibration checks if its probability percentages genuinely match reality at every confidence level.
definition_bullets: Prediction Bias measures the systematic gap between the average prediction and the average true outcome.
Calibration evaluates whether predicted probability values match actual observed event frequencies.
Reliability diagrams plot predicted confidence against observed positive rates along the diagonal y = x.
Post-hoc calibration techniques like Platt Scaling and Isotonic Regression adjust probabilities without retraining.

core_terms.what_is_it: A systematic directional error where predictions consistently overestimate or underestimate reality.
core_terms.definition: Prediction bias is the difference between the average predicted value and the average observed value across a dataset (Avg(Y_hat) - Avg(Y)).
core_terms.analogy: A bathroom scale that consistently adds 5 pounds to everyone's weight.
core_terms.why_it_matters: A non-zero bias reveals structural bugs such as training data distribution drift or uncalibrated loss functions.

core_terms.what_is_it: The alignment between a model's predicted confidence score and the true empirical likelihood of the event.
core_terms.definition: Calibration is the statistical property where among instances assigned a predicted probability p, the true empirical event frequency is exactly p.
core_terms.analogy: A doctor stating a surgery has an 80% success rate, and 8 out of 10 such patients truly recover.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Essential for risk management, medical triage, and automated pricing where probability values drive decisions.

core_terms.what_is_it: A visual plot comparing binned predicted probabilities against actual observed positive event rates.
core_terms.definition: A graphical diagnostic tool where predictions are grouped into quantile bins, plotting mean predicted probability on the x-axis against true observed frequency on the y-axis against the diagonal y = x.
core_terms.analogy: A flight gauge verifying that an airspeed indicator matches real aerodynamic speed.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Instantly identifies whether a classifier is overconfident, underconfident, or well-calibrated across all risk tiers.

core_terms.what_is_it: A strictly proper scoring rule measuring the mean squared difference between predicted probabilities and binary outcomes.
core_terms.definition: The Brier score is the mean squared error of probability forecasts, formulated as (1/N) * sum((p_hat_i - y_i)^2), where 0.0 indicates perfect accuracy and calibration.
core_terms.analogy: A scorecard that penalizes forecasters heavily for being confident and wrong.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Jointly evaluates discrimination and calibration into a single continuous optimization metric.

core_terms.what_is_it: A post-processing method that fits a logistic regression model to transform uncalibrated raw scores into true probabilities.
core_terms.definition: A calibration technique that fits a scalar sigmoid transformation over model outputs using a held-out calibration dataset.
core_terms.analogy: Adjusting a volume knob to ensure decibel readouts match actual sound pressure.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Effectively repairs the distorted, overconfident margins produced by Support Vector Machines and boosting models.

symbol_guide.description: Systematic directional difference: Avg(Predictions) - Avg(Actuals).
Actual observed value (continuous for regression, 0 or 1 for binary classification).
Continuous predicted numerical value in regression tasks.
Continuous probability score assigned to the positive class (0.0 to 1.0).
Mean squared probability error: (1/N) * sum((p_hat_i - y_i)^2).
Weighted average gap between bin confidence and bin empirical accuracy.
Subset of predictions falling into probability interval m.
Total number of evaluated samples across the evaluation dataset.

formula: $$\begin{aligned} \text{Prediction Bias (Regression)} &= \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N (\hat{y}_i - y_i) = \bar{\hat{y}} - \bar{y} \\[8pt] \text{Probability Bias (Classification)} &= \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \hat{p}_i - \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N y_i = \bar{\hat{p}} - \bar{y} \\[8pt] \text{Brier Score (BS)} &= \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N (\hat{p}_i - y_i)^2, \quad \text{ECE} = \sum_{m=1}^M \frac{|B_m|}{N} \left| \text{acc}(B_m) - \text{conf}(B_m) \right| \end{aligned}$$
logic: A model can have zero prediction bias while suffering from disastrous calibration. For example, if a model predicts 0.90 for low-risk meters (actual rate 0.10) and predicts 0.10 for high-risk meters (actual rate 0.90), its aggregate average prediction equals the ground truth average (0.50), resulting in zero bias. However, its individual probabilities are completely inverted and dangerously misleading. Calibration inspects conditional expectations P(Y=1 | P_hat=p) = p, guaranteeing that probability outputs are truthful across every confidence tier.
example: An energy utility uses an ML classifier to estimate electricity theft probability. If the model outputs a 70% probability for 1,000 smart meters, exactly 700 meters must genuinely exhibit theft for the utility to dispatch an audit workforce efficiently. If only 350 meters have theft, the model is severely overconfident: the utility wastes half its field budget investigating false alarms caused by uncalibrated probability numbers.
numerical_example:
Step-by-Step Worked Example (Electricity Forecasting & Theft Calibration):

1. Numerical Prediction Bias (3 Electricity Customers):
   - Customer A: Actual = 100 kWh, Predicted = 120 kWh (Error = +20)
   - Customer B: Actual = 200 kWh, Predicted = 220 kWh (Error = +20)
   - Customer C: Actual = 300 kWh, Predicted = 320 kWh (Error = +20)
   - Bias = (1/3) * [(120 - 100) + (220 - 200) + (320 - 300)] = 60 / 3 = +20.0 kWh
   - Diagnosis: Systematic overprediction by 20 units across the board.

2. Classification Probability Bias (1,000 Evaluated Meters):
   - Average Predicted Theft Probability: Mean(p_hat) = 0.30 (30.0%)
   - Actual Ground-Truth Theft Rate: Mean(y) = 0.10 (10.0%)
   - Aggregate Probability Bias = 0.30 - 0.10 = +0.20 (+20.0%)
   - Diagnosis: The model predicts three times more theft volume than actual reality.

3. Reliability Diagram Binning Analysis (Checking Calibration Across Tiers):
   - Bin 1 (0.00 - 0.20): Mean Predicted = 0.10, Observed Rate = 0.09 -> Well Calibrated (|Gap| = 0.01)
   - Bin 2 (0.20 - 0.40): Mean Predicted = 0.30, Observed Rate = 0.31 -> Well Calibrated (|Gap| = 0.01)
   - Bin 3 (0.40 - 0.60): Mean Predicted = 0.50, Observed Rate = 0.35 -> Overconfident (|Gap| = 0.15)
   - Bin 4 (0.70 - 0.90): Mean Predicted = 0.80, Observed Rate = 0.75 -> Slight Overprediction (|Gap| = 0.05)

4. Brier Score Calculation on Single Outcomes:
   - Case 1 (Actual Theft y = 1):
     * High confidence prediction p_hat = 0.90: Squared Error = (0.90 - 1)^2 = 0.010
     * Poor confidence prediction p_hat = 0.20: Squared Error = (0.20 - 1)^2 = 0.640
   - Case 2 (Total Brier Score across N samples):
     * Lower score indicates superior probabilistic accuracy (0.0 is perfect).

quick_types.name: Platt Scaling (Sigmoid Method)
quick_types.description: Fits a parametric logistic sigmoid over model output scores; ideal for small datasets.

quick_types.name: Isotonic Regression
quick_types.description: Fits a non-parametric, piece-wise monotonic staircase mapping; requires larger datasets.

quick_types.name: Underconfident Model Regime
quick_types.description: Reliability curve lies above the diagonal y = x; observed positive rate exceeds predicted confidence.

quick_types.name: Overconfident Model Regime
quick_types.description: Reliability curve lies below the diagonal y = x; predicted confidence exceeds true occurrence rate.

connected_logic.title: Zero Bias Does Not Guarantee Calibration
points: Positive and negative errors cancel out in global bias averages.
A model can overpredict low risk and underpredict high risk, yielding zero net bias.
Calibration verifies accuracy across each distinct probability slice.

connected_logic.title: Modern Neural Network Calibration Defect
points: Deep neural networks and boosted trees often output overconfident probabilities.
Cross-entropy loss pushes softmax logits toward extreme 0.0 or 1.0 values.
Models achieve high test accuracy while exhibiting poor probability calibration.

connected_logic.title: Post-Hoc Recalibration Protocol
points: Never calibrate on the training set: calibration models will trivially overfit.
Use a held-out validation split or CalibratedClassifierCV with cross-validation.
Re-evaluates probabilities on a separate test set to verify true generalization.

connected_logic.title: Scikit-Learn Implementation Standard
points: Compute calibration curves via calibration_curve(y_true, y_prob, n_bins=10).
Recalibrate estimators using CalibratedClassifierCV(method='sigmoid', cv=5).
Quantify probabilistic error using brier_score_loss(y_true, y_prob).

pitfalls: Confusing accuracy with calibration: An 85% accurate model can still output completely misleading probability values.
Calibrating on training data: Fitting Platt scaling on training logits causes severe overfitting and optimistic curves.
Small bin sample distortion: Evaluating calibration curves on sparse bins creates noisy, misleading fluctuations.
Assuming calibration alters ranking: Calibration transforms probability values monotonically without changing ROC-AUC or ranking.
Mistaking Brier score for pure calibration: Brier score reflects both sharpness (discrimination) and calibration combined.
key_takeaways: Prediction bias measures systematic over- or under-estimation across the entire dataset.
Calibration ensures that predicted probabilities match observed empirical frequencies at all confidence levels.
Reliability diagrams visually reveal whether a classifier is overconfident or underconfident along y = x.
Use Platt Scaling or Isotonic Regression via CalibratedClassifierCV to repair distorted probability outputs.

title: ROC Curve (TPR vs FPR)
def: A fundamental evaluation graph in classification that displays model diagnostic performance across all possible decision thresholds by plotting True Positive Rate (Sensitivity) on the y-axis against False Positive Rate (Fall-out) on the x-axis.
definition: A fundamental evaluation graph in classification that displays model diagnostic performance across all possible decision thresholds by plotting True Positive Rate (Sensitivity) on the y-axis against False Positive Rate (Fall-out) on the x-axis.
simple_summary: When a model outputs probabilities, choosing a single 50% cutoff is arbitrary. The Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve tests every possible threshold from 0% to 100% all at once. It plots how many real targets you catch (TPR) against how many false alarms you trigger (FPR). The closer the curve arches toward the top-left corner, the better the model separates good from bad.
definition_bullets: Plots True Positive Rate (Recall) on the y-axis against False Positive Rate on the x-axis.
Traces every possible decision threshold from 1.0 down to 0.0 continuously.
The top-left coordinate (0, 1) represents an ideal classifier with zero false alarms and 100% recall.
The 45-degree diagonal line represents the baseline performance of completely random guessing.

core_terms.what_is_it: A graphical curve mapping detection capability across every possible classification threshold.
core_terms.definition: The ROC curve is an evaluation plot created by computing True Positive Rate and False Positive Rate across all continuous classification threshold cutoffs.
core_terms.analogy: A radar technician testing every dial sensitivity to see how many incoming planes are spotted versus radar clutter.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Allows engineers to evaluate model discrimination power independently of any single operating threshold.

core_terms.what_is_it: The fraction of actual positive events successfully caught by the model.
core_terms.definition: The ratio of True Positives to all actual ground-truth positive cases (TP / (TP + FN)), plotted on the vertical y-axis.
core_terms.analogy: The percentage of actual power thieves that the utility inspection catches.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Represents the benefit axis, measuring total target capture coverage.

core_terms.what_is_it: The fraction of normal negative instances that were falsely flagged as positive.
core_terms.definition: The ratio of False Positives to all actual ground-truth negative cases (FP / (FP + TN)), plotted on the horizontal x-axis.
core_terms.analogy: The percentage of honest, law-abiding homeowners wrongly targeted for an inspection.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Represents the cost axis, measuring the rate of false alarms inflicted on normal populations.

core_terms.what_is_it: A single coordinate (FPR, TPR) on the ROC curve produced by choosing one specific threshold.
core_terms.definition: The specific (FPR, TPR) trade-off coordinate realized when a deployment threshold tau is chosen to convert probabilities into binary labels.
core_terms.analogy: A thermostat set to exactly 72 degrees balancing furnace running time with indoor comfort.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Represents the real-world operational trade-off experienced by production users.

core_terms.what_is_it: The diagonal line from (0,0) to (1,1) representing zero discrimination capability.
core_terms.definition: The line y = x where TPR equals FPR at every threshold, equivalent to flipping a coin to make predictions.
core_terms.analogy: A security guard guessing randomly at an entrance gate.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Provides the baseline benchmark; any useful ML model must curve significantly above this diagonal.

symbol_guide.description: Proportion of positive cases caught: TP / (TP + FN) = Recall.
Proportion of negative cases falsely flagged: FP / (FP + TN) = 1 - Specificity.
Probability threshold parameter sweeping across the continuum from 1.0 to 0.0.
Positive cases accurately labeled positive at threshold tau.
Negative cases incorrectly labeled positive at threshold tau.
Negative cases accurately labeled negative at threshold tau.
Positive cases incorrectly labeled negative at threshold tau.
Integral of the ROC curve quantifying overall ranking quality.

formula: $$\begin{aligned} y\text{-axis: } \text{TPR}(\tau) &= \frac{\text{TP}(\tau)}{\text{TP}(\tau) + \text{FN}(\tau)} = \text{Sensitivity} = \text{Recall} \\[8pt] x\text{-axis: } \text{FPR}(\tau) &= \frac{\text{FP}(\tau)}{\text{FP}(\tau) + \text{TN}(\tau)} = 1 - \text{Specificity} \\[8pt] \text{Ideal Point} &= (0.0, 1.0), \quad \text{Random Baseline: } y = x \end{aligned}$$
logic: Every threshold tau produces a different confusion matrix and therefore a single point (FPR, TPR) in ROC space. At tau = 1.0, the model predicts negative for everyone: TPR = 0 and FPR = 0 (the origin). As tau decreases toward 0.0, the model predicts positive for more instances, moving upward and rightward along the curve. At tau = 0.0, everyone is labeled positive: TPR = 1.0 and FPR = 1.0 (the top-right). A strong model pushes the curve sharply toward the top-left corner (0, 1), accumulating high TPR while keeping FPR near zero.
example: An electricity utility evaluates smart meter tampering across 1,000 meters (100 thefts, 900 normal). At a high threshold tau=0.80, the model catches 40 thefts (TPR=40%) with 0 false alarms (FPR=0%). Lowering tau to 0.50 captures 80 thefts (TPR=80%) while creating 30 false alarms (FPR=3.33%). Lowering tau further to 0.20 captures 98 thefts (TPR=98%) but generates 200 false alarms (FPR=22.2%). The ROC curve traces this exact path, allowing the utility to pick the optimal threshold for its budget.
numerical_example:
Step-by-Step Worked Example (Electricity Theft ROC Operating Point):

1. Confusion Matrix Evaluation at Operating Threshold tau = 0.50:
   - Actual Theft Meters (Positives): TP = 80, FN = 20 (Total = 100)
   - Actual Normal Meters (Negatives): FP = 30, TN = 870 (Total = 900)
   - Total Population Evaluated: N = 1,000 meters

2. Step 1: Calculate True Positive Rate (Y-Axis Coordinate):
   - TPR = TP / (TP + FN) = 80 / (80 + 20) = 80 / 100 = 0.800 (80.0%)
   - Interpretation: The model successfully captures 80% of all genuine theft cases.

3. Step 2: Calculate False Positive Rate (X-Axis Coordinate):
   - FPR = FP / (FP + TN) = 30 / (30 + 870) = 30 / 900 ≈ 0.0333 (3.33%)
   - Specificity = 1 - FPR = 870 / 900 = 0.9667 (96.67%)
   - Interpretation: The model triggers false alarms on only 3.33% of honest customers.

4. Step 3: Identify the ROC Coordinate:
   - Operating Point (x, y) = (FPR, TPR) = (0.0333, 0.8000)
   - Position in Plot: Close to the desirable top-left quadrant, well above the diagonal y = x.

5. Threshold Sweep Trajectory:
   - Threshold tau = 0.90 -> (FPR = 0.005, TPR = 0.35) -> Conservative
   - Threshold tau = 0.50 -> (FPR = 0.033, TPR = 0.80) -> Balanced
   - Threshold tau = 0.20 -> (FPR = 0.150, TPR = 0.95) -> Aggressive
   - The curve smoothly connects these coordinates across all possible probability thresholds.

quick_types.name: Near-Ideal Classifier (AUC > 0.95)
quick_types.description: Curves steeply along the left axis toward (0, 1), achieving near-perfect class separation.

quick_types.name: Good Operational Model (AUC 0.80 - 0.90)
quick_types.description: Strong upward arch with high TPR available at low, manageable FPR rates.

quick_types.name: Random Guessing Baseline (AUC = 0.50)
quick_types.description: Hugs the diagonal line y = x, indicating zero discrimination between positive and negative classes.

quick_types.name: Inverted Classifier (AUC < 0.50)
quick_types.description: Dips below the diagonal line; reversing model output probabilities fixes the inverted labels.

connected_logic.title: Threshold Invariance Property
points: ROC curves evaluate ranking quality across every potential threshold.
Decouples model evaluation from arbitrary single-point cutoff decisions.
Enables stakeholders to pick the optimal threshold after reviewing operational costs.

connected_logic.title: Scale Invariance Characteristic
points: ROC measures relative rank ordering rather than raw probability values.
Multiplying model logits by a constant does not change the ROC curve.
A model can possess a high AUC while exhibiting poor probability calibration.

connected_logic.title: Severe Class Imbalance Vulnerability
points: FPR divides by the negative class size: FP / (FP + TN).
When negatives are massive (1,000,000 normal meters), 1% FPR represents 10,000 false alarms.
A low FPR can deceptively mask an overwhelming avalanche of false alarms.

connected_logic.title: Scikit-Learn Implementation Standard
points: Generate curve via fpr, tpr, thresholds = roc_curve(y_true, y_scores).
Input must be continuous probabilities or decision function outputs, never binary labels.
Pass pos_label=1 when working with custom string or non-integer class labels.

pitfalls: Passing hard binary predictions: Passing 0/1 predictions produces a crude 3-point step instead of a smooth curve.
The class imbalance illusion: On 1% positive datasets, a low FPR masks thousands of false alarms; use PR curves instead.
Assuming ROC-AUC reflects calibration: A model with a great ROC curve can still output severely uncalibrated probabilities.
Confusing FPR with Precision: FPR divides by true negatives (FP/(FP+TN)), whereas Precision divides by predicted positives (TP/(TP+FP)).
Deploying without picking a threshold: The ROC curve displays all thresholds, but production software requires a single operating cutoff.
key_takeaways: The ROC curve plots True Positive Rate (Recall) against False Positive Rate across all classification thresholds.
Curves arching closer to the top-left corner (0, 1) indicate superior model separation capability.
The 45-degree diagonal represents random guessing with an AUC of 0.50.
On heavily imbalanced datasets, always pair the ROC curve with a Precision-Recall curve to monitor false alarm volume.

title: AUC-ROC (Area Under the ROC Curve)
def: A scalar classification metric representing the integral area under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve, quantifying a model's overall capability to rank positive instances above negative instances across all possible decision thresholds.
definition: A scalar classification metric representing the integral area under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve, quantifying a model's overall capability to rank positive instances above negative instances across all possible decision thresholds.
simple_summary: While the ROC curve is a full graph, AUC-ROC condenses that entire graph into a single number between 0 and 1. If an electricity theft detector has an AUC of 0.89, it means there is an 88.9% chance it will assign a higher suspiciousness score to a real thief than to an honest customer. A score of 0.5 is no better than flipping a coin, while 1.0 is flawless.
definition_bullets: Summarizes the entire Receiver Operating Characteristic curve into a single scalar value between 0.0 and 1.0.
Statistically equivalent to the probability that a random positive sample is scored higher than a random negative sample.
Completely threshold-independent: evaluates model ranking ability before choosing any cutoff.
A score of 0.50 denotes random guessing; scores above 0.85 indicate strong production-grade discrimination.

core_terms.term: Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC-ROC / AUROC)
core_terms.what_is_it: The integrated two-dimensional area beneath the ROC curve from FPR = 0 to FPR = 1.
core_terms.definition: AUC-ROC is the definite integral of the True Positive Rate with respect to the False Positive Rate over the unit interval [0, 1].
core_terms.analogy: The overall batting average of a baseball player across all pitchers and games.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Provides a universal, threshold-independent ranking benchmark to compare competing classifiers.

core_terms.what_is_it: The likelihood that a randomly drawn positive sample receives a higher score than a random negative sample.
core_terms.definition: The statistical equivalency proving AUC equals the probability P(score(positive) > score(negative)) + 0.5 * P(tie), identical to normalized Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney rank sums.
core_terms.analogy: Pitting every thief head-to-head against every honest customer in a tournament and counting wins.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Provides an intuitive, interview-ready mathematical meaning for what an AUC score actually measures.

core_terms.what_is_it: A metric property evaluating model sorting quality without fixing a single decision boundary.
core_terms.definition: The evaluation characteristic where performance is measured across all possible decision thresholds simultaneously rather than at a single operating point.
core_terms.analogy: Grading a stereo system on its entire frequency range rather than at just one volume setting.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Allows data scientists to compare model architectures before operations teams commit to an operating cutoff.

core_terms.what_is_it: The performance of a non-informative model that cannot distinguish positive from negative cases.
core_terms.definition: The line y = x where the model has exactly a 50/50 chance of correctly ordering pairs, bounding a triangular area of 0.50.
core_terms.analogy: Flipping a fair coin to decide which electricity meter to inspect.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Any useful machine learning model must perform significantly higher than 0.50 to justify deployment.

core_terms.what_is_it: A model whose predictions correlate negatively with the ground truth labels.
core_terms.definition: A model configuration where AUC drops below 0.50, indicating the model reliably assigns higher scores to negative instances than positive ones.
core_terms.analogy: A compass whose needle consistently points South instead of North.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Signifies inverted class labels (0 and 1 swapped); inverting predictions (1 - p) instantly flips the AUC to 1 - AUC.

symbol_guide.description: Scalar metric between 0.0 and 1.0 representing the integral under the ROC curve.
Predicted probability score assigned to an actual ground-truth positive instance.
Predicted probability score assigned to an actual ground-truth negative instance.
Total number of actual positive examples in the dataset.
Total number of actual negative examples in the dataset.
Total number of possible positive-negative sample comparisons.
Count of pairwise comparisons where the positive sample outranks the negative sample.
Operating probability cutoff evaluated across the full sweep interval.

formula: $$\begin{aligned} \text{AUC-ROC} &= \int_0^1 \text{TPR}(\text{FPR}^{-1}(u)) \, du = P(\hat{s}^+ > \hat{s}^-) + \frac{1}{2} P(\hat{s}^+ = \hat{s}^-) \\[8pt] \text{Pairwise Formulation} &= \frac{1}{N^+ N^-} \sum_{i=1}^{N^+} \sum_{j=1}^{N^-} \mathbb{I}(\hat{s}_i^+ > \hat{s}_j^-) = \frac{U}{N^+ N^-} \end{aligned}$$
logic: AUC-ROC evaluates relative ordering, not absolute calibration. If every positive score is 0.51 and every negative score is 0.49, the model achieves a perfect AUC of 1.00 because all positive samples rank above negative ones. Similarly, scaling or shifting probability scores monotonically leaves AUC completely unchanged. AUC measures separation purity: how clean is the margin between the positive score distribution and the negative score distribution.
example: A fraud detection team evaluates two models for electricity theft detection. Model A has an AUC of 0.89, while Model B has an AUC of 0.65. When testing 9 positive-negative consumer pairs, Model A ranks the true thief higher in 8 out of 9 comparisons. Model B only gets 6 out of 9 correct. Even before choosing whether to dispatch audits at 50% or 70% probability, Model A is proven to be a fundamentally superior ranker.
numerical_example:
Step-by-Step Worked Example (Pairwise Mann-Whitney U Computation):

1. Test Dataset (6 Electricity Meters):
   - Actual Theft Cases (Positives):
     * Meter A: score = 0.90
     * Meter B: score = 0.80
     * Meter C: score = 0.40
   - Actual Normal Cases (Negatives):
     * Meter D: score = 0.70
     * Meter E: score = 0.30
     * Meter F: score = 0.10

2. Pairwise Matrix Analysis (N+ = 3, N- = 3 -> Total Pairs = 3 * 3 = 9):
   - Meter A (0.90) vs Normal Meters:
     * A vs D (0.90 > 0.70) -> Win (1)
     * A vs E (0.90 > 0.30) -> Win (1)
     * A vs F (0.90 > 0.10) -> Win (1) -> Subtotal = 3 wins
   - Meter B (0.80) vs Normal Meters:
     * B vs D (0.80 > 0.70) -> Win (1)
     * B vs E (0.80 > 0.30) -> Win (1)
     * B vs F (0.80 > 0.10) -> Win (1) -> Subtotal = 3 wins
   - Meter C (0.40) vs Normal Meters:
     * C vs D (0.40 < 0.70) -> Loss (0)
     * C vs E (0.40 > 0.30) -> Win (1)
     * C vs F (0.40 > 0.10) -> Win (1) -> Subtotal = 2 wins

3. Final AUC-ROC Calculation:
   - Total Correctly Ordered Pairs = 3 + 3 + 2 = 8 wins
   - Total Evaluated Pairs = 9 pairs
   - AUC-ROC = Wins / Total Pairs = 8 / 9 ≈ 0.8889 (88.9%)
   - Interpretation: If a random thief and a random normal meter are selected, the model ranks the thief higher 88.9% of the time.

quick_types.name: Exceptional Discrimination (0.90 - 1.00)
quick_types.description: Near-flawless rank ordering; positive instances almost always score higher than negative ones.

quick_types.name: Good Discrimination (0.80 - 0.89)
quick_types.description: Standard industry benchmark for production fraud, churn, and recommendation systems.

quick_types.name: Fair Discrimination (0.70 - 0.79)
quick_types.description: Acceptable for noisy real-world problems like marketing propensity or macro forecasting.

quick_types.name: Non-Informative / Inverted (< 0.50 - 0.50)
quick_types.description: 0.50 denotes random guessing; sub-0.50 indicates inverted labels requiring sign reversal.

connected_logic.title: Threshold Agnostic vs Operational Deployment
points: AUC-ROC measures global ranking without fixing a single decision boundary.
High AUC does not specify which operating threshold to deploy in production.
Operations teams must select an operating point (tau) based on business costs.

connected_logic.title: Independence from Probability Calibration
points: Monotonic score transformations (e.g. squaring probabilities) leave AUC unchanged.
A model can possess an AUC of 0.95 while outputting completely uncalibrated probabilities.
Evaluate Brier score or reliability curves if raw probabilities drive automated actions.

connected_logic.title: Class Imbalance Blind Spot
points: AUC-ROC is insensitive to class prevalence because FPR normalizes by total negatives.
On a 99.9% negative dataset, 0.90 AUC can still produce thousands of false alarms.
In highly skewed fraud and medical datasets, prioritize Precision-Recall AUC (PR-AUC).

connected_logic.title: Scikit-Learn Implementation Standard
points: Computed via roc_auc_score(y_true, y_scores).
Always supply continuous prediction probabilities (predict_proba[:, 1]), never binary 0/1 labels.
Multi-class classification supports average='macro' or 'weighted' with multi_class='ovr'.

pitfalls: Passing hard binary predictions: Supplying 0/1 labels replaces smooth ranking with coarse trapezoids, deflating AUC.
The high AUC false security trap: An AUC of 0.92 on rare fraud can still flood investigators with 90% false alarms.
Mistaking AUC for accuracy: AUC = 0.85 means 85% pairwise ranking probability, not 85% correct predictions.
Ignoring inverted labels: An AUC of 0.15 means the model is actually 85% accurate, but labels are inverted.
Neglecting business error costs: AUC weights errors across all thresholds equally, even irrelevant extreme regions.
key_takeaways: AUC-ROC summarizes the entire ROC curve into a single threshold-independent ranking metric.
Statistically, AUC represents the probability that a random positive example is ranked higher than a random negative.
A score of 0.50 is equivalent to random guessing, while 1.00 denotes perfect class separation.
Always evaluate AUC-ROC alongside Precision-Recall metrics when working with severe class imbalance.

title: Precision-Recall (PR) Curve
def: An essential classification evaluation graph that plots Precision on the vertical y-axis against Recall on the horizontal x-axis across all decision thresholds, exposing false alarm vulnerabilities on highly imbalanced datasets.
definition: An essential classification evaluation graph that plots Precision on the vertical y-axis against Recall on the horizontal x-axis across all decision thresholds, exposing false alarm vulnerabilities on highly imbalanced datasets.
simple_summary: When looking for rare events like credit card fraud or electricity theft, 99% of people are innocent. A standard ROC curve can look deceptively great while still burying investigators in thousands of false alarms. The Precision-Recall (PR) curve exposes this reality by checking: out of everyone you accused, how many were actually guilty (Precision), and how many total guilty people did you catch (Recall)?
definition_bullets: Plots Precision on the y-axis against Recall on the x-axis across all possible thresholds.
The ideal performance coordinate is the top-right corner (1.0 Recall, 1.0 Precision).
The baseline for a random guessing model equals the positive class prevalence (e.g., 0.05 for 5% rare events).
Ignores True Negatives entirely, preventing massive negative majorities from distorting evaluation.

core_terms.what_is_it: A diagnostic plot visualizing the trade-off between prediction purity and positive event coverage.
core_terms.definition: The PR curve is a graphical evaluation mapping Precision against Recall computed across a continuous spectrum of probability decision thresholds.
core_terms.analogy: A metal detector's trade-off between beeping only for pure gold versus catching every buried coin.
core_terms.why_it_matters: The premier evaluation graph for rare-event detection where false positives carry immediate operational costs.

core_terms.what_is_it: A single scalar summarizing the entire PR curve as a recall-weighted average of precision.
core_terms.definition: Average Precision is the area under the interpolated precision-recall curve calculated as the sum of precision at each threshold multiplied by the increase in recall (Sum (R_n - R_{n-1}) * P_n).
core_terms.analogy: A student's GPA weighted by credit hours rather than a simple unweighted test score average.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Provides an objective scalar metric to rank competing models on highly imbalanced classification tasks.

core_terms.what_is_it: The performance of a random classifier on a PR curve, equal to the proportion of positive samples.
core_terms.definition: The horizontal line y = P / (P + N) representing the precision of a random guesser on the PR curve.
core_terms.analogy: A lottery ticket whose winning odds equal the proportion of winning tickets in the bucket.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Unlike ROC's fixed 0.50 diagonal baseline, PR baseline shifts based on dataset rarity.

core_terms.what_is_it: The inverse behavioral relationship where increasing recall typically reduces precision.
core_terms.definition: The structural operational trade-off where lowering decision thresholds captures more genuine positive instances (higher recall) while inviting more false alarms (lower precision).
core_terms.analogy: Casting a wider fishing net that catches more fish but scoops up extra seaweed and trash.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Forces engineering teams to select an operational threshold aligned with available audit budgets.

core_terms.what_is_it: Two slightly different mathematical methods for calculating the scalar area under the PR curve.
core_terms.definition: PR-AUC uses trapezoidal numerical integration (often overly optimistic due to linear interpolation), whereas AP uses rectangular step-wise recall increments (the scikit-learn standard).
core_terms.analogy: Measuring a jagged shoreline with a straight ruler versus following exact discrete footsteps.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Scikit-learn deprecated trapezoidal auc(recall, precision) in favor of average_precision_score to avoid optimistic bias.

symbol_guide.description: Proportion of positive alerts that are genuine: TP / (TP + FP).
Proportion of actual positive cases successfully caught: TP / (TP + FN).
Discrete recall-weighted average precision score across all thresholds.
Recall value computed at evaluation rank threshold step n.
Precision value computed at evaluation rank threshold step n.
Proportion of true positive cases in the population: P / (P + N).
Probability threshold applied to convert continuous scores to binary predictions.

formula: $$\begin{aligned} y\text{-axis: } \text{Precision}(\tau) &= \frac{\text{TP}(\tau)}{\text{TP}(\tau) + \text{FP}(\tau)} \\[8pt] x\text{-axis: } \text{Recall}(\tau) &= \frac{\text{TP}(\tau)}{\text{TP}(\tau) + \text{FN}(\tau)} \\[8pt] \text{Average Precision (AP)} &= \sum_{n=1}^K (R_n - R_{n-1}) P_n, \quad \text{Random Baseline} = \pi = \frac{P}{P + N} \end{aligned}$$
logic: Why is the PR curve superior to ROC on imbalanced datasets? The ROC curve's x-axis is FPR = FP / (FP + TN). When TN is massive (e.g., 990,000 legitimate bank transactions), having 1,000 false alarms results in an FPR of barely 0.1%, giving a falsely glowing ROC curve. In contrast, the PR curve's y-axis is Precision = TP / (TP + FP). If there were only 100 true frauds, having 1,000 false alarms crashes precision down to 100 / (100 + 1000) ≈ 9.1%. The PR curve exposes the operational crisis that ROC completely hides.
example: An electricity provider monitors 1,000 meters where 100 are true thefts and 900 are normal. At an operating threshold tau = 0.50, the model detects 80 thefts (Recall = 80%) but triggers 120 false alarms. The ROC curve shows a comfortable FPR of 120 / 900 = 13.3%. However, the PR curve reveals a sobering reality: Precision is only 80 / (80 + 120) = 40.0%. For every 10 technicians sent to investigate, 6 find innocent customers, wasting 60% of the utility's field inspection budget.
numerical_example:
Step-by-Step Worked Example (Electricity Theft PR Evaluation):

1. Dataset Ground Truth (1,000 Evaluated Meters):
   - Actual Theft Meters (Positive P): 100 meters (10% prevalence)
   - Actual Normal Meters (Negative N): 900 meters (90% base rate)
   - Base Rate Baseline: pi = 100 / 1,000 = 0.10 (10.0%)

2. Confusion Matrix at Threshold tau = 0.50:
   - TP = 80, FN = 20 (Actual Thefts = 100)
   - FP = 120, TN = 780 (Actual Normal = 900)
   - Total Predicted Thefts = TP + FP = 80 + 120 = 200 meters

3. Coordinate Calculation for Operating Point:
   - Recall (X-Axis) = TP / (TP + FN) = 80 / (80 + 20) = 80 / 100 = 0.80 (80.0%)
   - Precision (Y-Axis) = TP / (TP + FP) = 80 / (80 + 120) = 80 / 200 = 0.40 (40.0%)
   - PR Point (Recall, Precision) = (0.80, 0.40)
   - Operational Reality: High 80% coverage, but 60% of field audits are wasted false alarms.

4. Average Precision (AP) Step-by-Step Integration:
   - Threshold 0.90: Recall = 0.30, Precision = 0.90 -> (0.30 - 0.00) * 0.90 = 0.270
   - Threshold 0.70: Recall = 0.60, Precision = 0.75 -> (0.60 - 0.30) * 0.75 = 0.225
   - Threshold 0.50: Recall = 0.80, Precision = 0.40 -> (0.80 - 0.60) * 0.40 = 0.080
   - Threshold 0.20: Recall = 0.95, Precision = 0.25 -> (0.95 - 0.80) * 0.25 = 0.0375
   - Approximate AP = 0.270 + 0.225 + 0.080 + 0.0375 ≈ 0.6125 (61.3%)
   - Comparison: Far above random baseline (10.0%), but reveals sharp precision decay at high recall.

quick_types.name: Near-Ideal Classifier (AP > 0.90)
quick_types.description: Hugs the top-right corner; maintains near 100% precision even as recall approaches 1.0.

quick_types.name: Graceful Decay Model (AP 0.60 - 0.80)
quick_types.description: High precision at moderate recall, decaying steadily as the net widens to capture edge cases.

quick_types.name: Prevalence Baseline Model (AP ~ pi)
quick_types.description: A horizontal line at y = prevalence, representing a non-informative random classifier.

quick_types.name: Early Triage Regime (High Precision / Low Recall)
quick_types.description: Top-left segment of the curve; triggers automated high-confidence actions without human review.

connected_logic.title: Sensitivity to Positive Class Prevalence
points: ROC curves are invariant to class distribution changes.
PR curves shift dynamically when the positive event prevalence changes.
Directly reflects the real-world operational false alarm rate experienced by teams.

connected_logic.title: Threshold Moving Along the PR Curve
points: Moving leftward on the curve increases precision but sacrifices recall.
Moving rightward captures more total positive cases but degrades precision.
Helps teams select a threshold matching human investigator capacity.

connected_logic.title: Trap of Linear Interpolation in PR Space
points: Linear interpolation between PR coordinates creates overly optimistic curves.
Precision and recall do not vary linearly between decision thresholds.
Scikit-learn uses rectangular step functions (Average Precision) to ensure rigor.

connected_logic.title: Scikit-Learn Implementation Standard
points: Compute coordinates via precision_recall_curve(y_true, y_scores).
Note that precision and recall arrays have length n_thresholds + 1.
Always evaluate scalar summary using average_precision_score(y_true, y_scores).

pitfalls: Using trapezoidal integration for PR-AUC: Scikit-learn deprecated trapz on PR curves because it yields overly optimistic scores.
Relying on ROC curves for rare events: A 95% ROC-AUC can hide a disastrous 5% precision in fraud pipelines.
Assuming the baseline is 0.50: The random guessing baseline on a PR curve is the positive class prevalence (e.g. 0.02).
Passing binary predictions: Hard 0/1 predictions reduce the PR curve to a single crude triangle.
Forgetting that thresholds array has length n - 1: Precision and recall include boundary endpoints (0 and 1) not in thresholds.
key_takeaways: The PR curve plots Precision against Recall across all classification decision thresholds.
The PR curve is essential for evaluating models trained on imbalanced datasets with rare positive classes.
Average Precision (AP) summarizes the PR curve as a recall-weighted average of precision.
Curves closer to the top-right corner indicate a superior precision-recall trade-off.

title: Operating Point & Threshold Tuning
def: The operational post-processing practice in machine learning of selecting a specific probability cutoff to convert continuous model scores into discrete decisions, aligning model behavior with business constraints and asymmetric financial error costs.
definition: The operational post-processing practice in machine learning of selecting a specific probability cutoff to convert continuous model scores into discrete decisions, aligning model behavior with business constraints and asymmetric financial error costs.
simple_summary: Training a model only gives you probability scores from 0% to 100%. Deciding where to draw the line between 'normal' and 'theft' is threshold tuning. If sending an inspector costs ₹500 but catching a thief saves ₹5,000, you should not use the default 50% cutoff. Instead, you lower the threshold to catch more thieves, choosing the exact operating point that maximizes profit and minimizes wasted work.
definition_bullets: Converts continuous probability predictions into actionable binary classification decisions.
An operating point defines the exact combination of Precision, Recall, TPR, and FPR at a chosen threshold.
Threshold tuning moves the operating point along ROC/PR curves without retraining model weights.
Must always be tuned on a validation set and verified on an untouched test set to avoid leakage.

core_terms.what_is_it: The configurable numerical cutoff boundary that separates positive predictions from negative predictions.
core_terms.definition: The probability cutoff tau such that any instance with predicted probability p >= tau is classified as positive, and negative otherwise.
core_terms.analogy: The height requirement line at a theme park ride determining who gets on.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Allows business operators to alter model sensitivity without retraining weights or modifying code.

core_terms.what_is_it: The specific realized combination of classification metrics resulting from a single threshold choice.
core_terms.definition: The concrete coordinate on an ROC curve (FPR, TPR) or PR curve (Recall, Precision) established by selecting a specific threshold tau.
core_terms.analogy: Choosing a specific cruise control speed that balances travel time against fuel consumption.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Defines the day-to-day operational reality and workload experienced by field investigation teams.

core_terms.what_is_it: Selecting the threshold that minimizes total real-world financial losses from false alarms and missed events.
core_terms.definition: A threshold selection framework minimizing the expected cost function Cost(tau) = C_FP * FP(tau) + C_FN * FN(tau).
core_terms.analogy: Deciding whether to buy earthquake insurance based on damage probability multiplied by repair cost.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Bridges the gap between raw machine learning accuracy and real enterprise profitability.

core_terms.what_is_it: A mathematical criterion that picks the threshold maximizing the gap between true positives and false alarms.
core_terms.definition: A metric defined as J = TPR - FPR = Sensitivity + Specificity - 1, selecting the threshold furthest above the random diagonal.
core_terms.analogy: Finding the peak of a bell curve where benefits most exceed drawbacks.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Provides an objective statistical operating point when financial costs cannot be accurately quantified.

core_terms.what_is_it: Setting the decision threshold based strictly on the maximum volume of alerts a team can manually process.
core_terms.definition: A constraint-driven selection method where threshold tau is set to ensure the total flagged count (TP + FP) does not exceed physical operational capacity.
core_terms.analogy: Setting emergency room triage thresholds so doctors only admit as many trauma patients as there are open beds.
core_terms.why_it_matters: Prevents automated AI systems from overwhelming human investigation and audit teams with backlogs.

symbol_guide.description: Continuous cutoff parameter between 0.0 and 1.0 determining class assignment.
The specific threshold selected to optimize costs or business constraints.
Continuous score output by the model classifier for an instance.
Monetary or operational loss incurred by an unnecessary false alarm.
Monetary or operational loss incurred by failing to catch a true positive event.
Total false alarms generated when using threshold tau.
Total missed positive cases when using threshold tau.
Informedness metric: TPR(tau) - FPR(tau).

logic: Why is the default tau = 0.50 threshold rarely optimal? A 0.50 cutoff implicitly assumes two conditions: (1) false positives and false negatives cost exactly the same amount, and (2) positive and negative classes are balanced 50/50. In real applications, both assumptions fail. In electricity theft detection, missing an illegal bypass (C_FN = ₹5,000) costs 10 times more than an unnecessary inspection (C_FP = ₹500). Tuning the threshold shifts the operating point along the ROC/PR curve, optimizing financial returns without changing a single model parameter.
example: An electricity distribution utility monitors 1,000 smart meters. Inspecting an honest customer's meter costs C_FP = ₹500 in technician time. Missing an ongoing power theft leaks C_FN = ₹5,000 in unbilled power annually. Threshold A (tau = 0.35) produces 100 FPs and 10 FNs, totaling ₹1,00,000 in error costs. Threshold B (tau = 0.65) produces only 30 FPs but misses 25 thefts, costing ₹1,40,000. Threshold A is selected because it saves the utility ₹40,000 annually.
numerical_example:
Step-by-Step Worked Example (Electricity Theft Cost Optimization):

1. Toy Threshold Demonstration (5 Meters, True Thefts: A, B, D; Normal: C, E):
   - Meter A: 0.95 | Meter B: 0.82 | Meter C: 0.61 | Meter D: 0.35 | Meter E: 0.12
   - Case 1 (Standard Cutoff tau = 0.50):
     * Flagged (prob >= 0.50): Meters A, B, C (3 flagged)
     * Outcomes: TP = 2 (A, B), FP = 1 (C), FN = 1 (D missed)
     * Metrics: Precision = 2 / 3 = 66.7%, Recall = 2 / 3 = 66.7%
   - Case 2 (Lower Cutoff tau = 0.30):
     * Flagged (prob >= 0.30): Meters A, B, C, D (4 flagged)
     * Outcomes: TP = 3 (A, B, D caught), FP = 1 (C), FN = 0 (Zero misses!)
     * Metrics: Precision = 3 / 4 = 75.0%, Recall = 3 / 3 = 100.0%

2. Enterprise Financial Cost Evaluation (1,000 Evaluated Meters):
   - Cost of False Positive (Unnecessary field inspection): C_FP = ₹500
   - Cost of False Negative (Unbilled stolen power leakage): C_FN = ₹5,000
   - Cost Formula: Total Cost = (500 * FP) + (5,000 * FN)

3. Comparing Two Operating Points:
   - Operating Point A (Aggressive Cutoff tau = 0.35):
     * FP = 100, FN = 10
     * FP Expense = 100 * ₹500 = ₹50,000
     * FN Loss = 10 * ₹5,000 = ₹50,000
     * Total Financial Error Cost = ₹50,000 + ₹50,000 = ₹1,00,000
   - Operating Point B (Conservative Cutoff tau = 0.65):
     * FP = 30, FN = 25
     * FP Expense = 30 * ₹500 = ₹15,000
     * FN Loss = 25 * ₹5,000 = ₹1,25,000
     * Total Financial Error Cost = ₹15,000 + ₹1,25,000 = ₹1,40,000

4. Business Verdict:
   - Threshold A incurs more field inspections (100 vs 30) but saves ₹40,000 in net profit.
   - Operational tuning delivers a 28.6% cost reduction without retraining the underlying ML model.

quick_types.name: Cost-Minimizing Threshold
quick_types.description: Directly minimizes financial loss using explicit unit costs for false positives and false negatives.

quick_types.name: Constraint-Driven Threshold

quick_types.name: F1-Score Maximizing Threshold
quick_types.description: Finds the operating point with highest harmonic balance between precision and recall.

quick_types.name: Youden's J Statistic Threshold
